{{Short description|Construction in homological algebra}}
In [[mathematics]], the '''Tor functors''' are the [[derived functor]]s of the [[tensor product of modules]] over a [[ring (mathematics)|ring]]. Along with the [[Ext functor]], Tor is one of the central concepts of [[homological algebra]], in which ideas from [[algebraic topology]] are used to construct invariants of algebraic structures. The [[group cohomology#Group homology|homology of groups]], [[Lie algebra homology|Lie algebra]]s, and [[Hochschild homology|associative algebras]] can all be defined in terms of Tor. The name comes from a relation between the first Tor group Tor<sub>1</sub> and the [[torsion subgroup]] of an [[abelian group]].

In the special case of abelian groups, Tor was introduced by [[Eduard Čech]] in 1935<ref>{{Cite journal | author1-last=Čech | author1-first=Eduard | author1-link=Eduard Čech | title=Les groupes de Betti d'un complexe infini | journal=[[Fundamenta Mathematicae]] | volume=25 | year=1935 | pages=33–44 | doi=10.4064/fm-25-1-33-44 | jfm=61.0609.02| url=http://dml.cz/bitstream/handle/10338.dmlcz/501039/Cech_01-0000-67_1.pdf | doi-access=free }}</ref> and named by [[Samuel Eilenberg]] around 1950.<ref>Weibel (1999).</ref> It was first applied to the [[Künneth theorem]] and [[universal coefficient theorem]] in topology. For modules over any [[ring (mathematics)|ring]], Ext was defined by [[Henri Cartan]] and Eilenberg in 1956.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Cartan |first=Henri |title=Homological Algebra |last2=Eilenberg |first2=Samuel |publisher=Princeton University Press |year=1999 |isbn=0-691-04991-2 |edition= |mr=0575792 |orig-year=1956}}</ref>

==Definition==
Let <math>R</math> be a [[ring (mathematics)|ring]]. Write <math>R\textsf{-Mod}</math> for the [[category theory|category]] of [[module (mathematics)|left <math>R</math>-modules]] and <math>\textsf{Mod-}R</math> for the category of right <math>R</math>-modules. (If <math>R</math> is [[commutative ring|commutative]], the two categories can be identified.) For a fixed left <math>R</math>-module <math>B</math>, let <math>T(A) = A\otimes_R B</math> for <math>A</math> in <math>\textsf{Mod-}R</math>. This is a [[right exact functor]] from <math>\textsf{Mod-}R</math> to the [[category of abelian groups]] <math>\textbf{Ab}</math>, and so it has left [[derived functor]]s <math>\mathcal L_i T</math>. The Tor groups are the abelian groups defined by
<math display="block">\operatorname{Tor}_i^R(A,B) = (\mathcal L_iT)(A),</math>
for an [[integer]] <math>i</math>. By definition, this means: take any [[projective module#Projective resolutions|projective resolution]]
<math display="block">\cdots\to P_2 \to P_1 \to P_0 \to A\to 0,</math>
and remove <math>A</math>, and form the [[chain complex]]:
<math display="block">\cdots \to P_2\otimes_R B \to P_1\otimes_R B \to P_0\otimes_R B \to 0</math>

For each integer <math>i</math>, the group <math>\operatorname{Tor}_i^R(A,B)</math> is the [[chain complex|homology]] of this complex at position <math>i</math>. It is zero for <math>i</math> negative. Moreover, <math>\operatorname{Tor}_0^R(A,B)</math> is the [[cokernel]] of the map <math>P_1\otimes_R B \to P_0\otimes_R B</math>, which is [[isomorphic]] to <math>A \otimes_R B</math>.

Alternatively, one can define <math>\mathrm{Tor}</math> by fixing <math>A</math> and taking the left derived functors of the right exact functor <math>G(B)=A\otimes_RB</math>. That is, tensor <math>A</math> with a projective resolution of <math>B</math> and take homology. Cartan and Eilenberg showed that these constructions are independent of the choice of projective resolution, and that both constructions yield the same Tor groups.<ref>Weibel (1994), section 2.4 and Theorem 2.7.2.</ref> Moreover, for a fixed ring <math>R</math>, <math>\mathrm{Tor}</math> is a functor in each variable (from <math>R</math>-modules to abelian groups).

For a commutative ring <math>R</math> and <math>R</math>-modules <math>A</math> and <math>B</math>, <math>\operatorname{Tor}^R_i(A,B)</math> is an <math>R</math>-module (using that <math>A\otimes_RB</math> is an <math>R</math>-module in this case). For a non-commutative ring <math>R</math>, <math>\operatorname{Tor}^R_i(A,B)</math> is only an abelian group, in general. If <math>R</math> is an [[algebra over a ring]] <math>S</math> (which means in particular that <math>S</math> is commutative), then <math>\operatorname{Tor}^R_i(A,B)</math> is at least an <math>S</math>-module.

==Properties==
Here are some of the basic properties and computations of Tor groups.<ref>Weibel (1994), Chapters 2 and 3.</ref>

*<math>\mathrm{Tor}_0^R(A,B)\cong A\otimes_RB</math> for any right <math>R</math>-module <math>A</math> and left <math>R</math>-module <math>B</math>.
*<math>\mathrm{Tor}_i^R(A,B)=0</math> for all <math>i>0</math> if either <math>A</math> or <math>B</math> is [[flat module|flat]] (for example, [[free module|free]]) as an <math>R</math>-module. In fact, one can compute Tor using a flat resolution of either <math>A</math> or <math>B</math>; this is more general than a projective (or free) resolution.<ref>Weibel (1994), Lemma 3.2.8.</ref>
*If <math>A, B</math> are finitely generated abelian groups, then <math>\operatorname{Tor}_1^\Z(A,B) \cong A_{\text{tor}} \otimes_\Z B_{\text{tor}}</math>, where <math>A_{\text{tor}}</math> is the [[torsion subgroup]] of <math>A</math>.
*There are converses to the previous statement:
**If <math>\mathrm{Tor}_1^R(A,B)=0</math> for all <math>B</math>, then <math>A</math> is flat (and hence <math>\mathrm{Tor}_i^R(A,B)=0</math> for all <math>i>0</math>).
**If <math>\mathrm{Tor}_1^R(A,B)=0</math> for all <math>A</math>, then <math>B</math> is flat (and hence <math>\mathrm{Tor}_i^R(A,B)=0</math> for all <math>i>0</math>).
*By the general properties of [[derived functor]]s, every [[short exact sequence]] <math>0\to K\to L\to M\to 0</math> of right <math>R</math>-modules induces a [[long exact sequence]] of the form<ref>Weibel (1994), Definition 2.1.1.</ref> <math display="block">\cdots \to \operatorname{Tor}_2^R(M,B) \to \operatorname{Tor}_1^R(K,B) \to \operatorname{Tor}_1^R(L,B) \to \operatorname{Tor}_1^R (M,B) \to K\otimes_R B\to L\otimes_R B\to M\otimes_R B\to 0,</math> for any left <math>R</math>-module <math>B</math>. The analogous exact sequence also holds for Tor with respect to the second variable.
*Symmetry: for a commutative ring <math>R</math>, there is a [[natural isomorphism]] <math>\mathrm{Tor}_i^R(A,B)\cong \mathrm{Tor}_i^R(B,A)</math>.<ref>Weibel (1994), Remark in section 3.1.</ref> (For <math>R</math> commutative, there is no need to distinguish between left and right <math>R</math>-modules.)
*If <math>R</math> is a commutative ring and <math>u</math> in <math>R</math> is not a [[zero divisor]], then for any <math>R</math>-module <math>B</math>, <math display="block">\operatorname{Tor}^R_i(R/(u),B)\cong\begin{cases} B/uB & i=0\\ B[u] & i=1\\ 0 &\text{otherwise}\end{cases}</math> where <math display="block">B[u] = \{x \in B : ux =0 \}</math> is the <math>u</math>-torsion subgroup of <math>B</math>. This is the explanation for the name Tor. Taking <math>R</math> to be the ring <math>\Z</math> of integers, this calculation can be used to compute <math>\operatorname{Tor}^{\Z}_1(A,B)</math> for any [[finitely generated abelian group]] <math>A</math>.
*Generalizing the previous example, one can compute Tor groups that involve the quotient of a commutative ring by any [[regular sequence]], using the [[Koszul complex]].<ref>Weibel (1994), section 4.5.</ref> For example, if <math>R</math> is the [[polynomial ring]] <math>k[x_1,\ldots,x_n]</math> over a field <math>k</math>, then <math>\operatorname{Tor}_*^R(k,k)</math> is the [[exterior algebra]] over <math>k</math> on <math>n</math> generators in <math>\mathrm{Tor}_1</math>.
* <math>\operatorname{Tor}^{\Z}_i(A,B)=0</math> for all <math>i\ge 2</math>. The reason: every [[abelian group]] <math>A</math> has a free resolution of length 1, since every subgroup of a [[free abelian group]] is free abelian. 
* Generalizing the previous example, <math>\operatorname{Tor}^{R}_i(A,B)=0</math> for all <math>i\ge 2</math> if <math>R</math> is a [[principal ideal domain]] (PID). The reason: every module <math>A</math> over a PID has a free resolution of length 1, since every submodule of a [[free module]] over a PID is free. 
*For any ring <math>R</math>, Tor preserves [[direct sum of modules|direct sums]] (possibly infinite) and [[filtered colimit]]s in each variable.<ref>Weibel (1994), Corollary 2.6.17.</ref> For example, in the first variable, this says that <math display="block">\begin{align}
\operatorname{Tor}_i^R \left (\bigoplus_{\alpha} M_{\alpha}, N \right ) &\cong \bigoplus_{\alpha} \operatorname{Tor}_i^R(M_{\alpha},N) \\
\operatorname{Tor}_i^R \left (\varinjlim_{\alpha} M_{\alpha}, N \right ) &\cong \varinjlim_{\alpha} \operatorname{Tor}_i^R(M_{\alpha},N)
\end{align}</math>
*Flat base change: for a commutative flat <math>R</math>-algebra <math>T</math>, <math>R</math>-modules <math>A</math> and <math>B</math>, and an integer <math>i</math>,<ref>Weibel (1994), Corollary 3.2.10.</ref> <math display="block">\mathrm{Tor}_i^R(A,B)\otimes_R T \cong \mathrm{Tor}_i^T(A\otimes_R T,B\otimes_R T).</math> It follows that Tor commutes with [[localization of a ring|localization]]. That is, for a [[multiplicatively closed set]] <math>S</math> in <math>R</math>, <math display="block">S^{-1} \operatorname{Tor}_i^R(A, B) \cong \operatorname{Tor}_i^{S^{-1} R} \left (S^{-1} A, S^{-1} B \right ).</math>
*For a commutative ring <math>R</math> and commutative <math>R</math>-algebras <math>A</math> and <math>B</math>, <math>\mathrm{Tor}_*^R(A,B)</math> has the structure of a [[graded-commutative]] algebra over <math>R</math>. Moreover, elements of odd degree in the Tor algebra have square zero, and there are [[divided power]] operations on the elements of positive even degree.<ref>Avramov & Halperin (1986), section 2.16; {{Citation | title=Stacks Project, Tag 09PQ | url=http://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/09PQ}}.</ref>

==Important special cases==

*[[Group homology]] is defined by <math>H_*(G,M)=\operatorname{Tor}^{\Z[G]}_*(\Z, M),</math> where ''G'' is a group, ''M'' is a [[group representation|representation]] of ''G'' over the integers, and <math>\Z[G]</math> is the [[group ring]] of ''G''.
*For an [[algebra over a field|algebra]] ''A'' over a field ''k'' and an ''A''-[[bimodule]] ''M'', [[Hochschild homology]] is defined by <math display="block">HH_*(A,M)=\operatorname{Tor}_*^{A\otimes_k A^{\text{op}}}(A, M).</math>
*[[Lie algebra homology]] is defined by <math>H_*(\mathfrak g,M)=\operatorname{Tor}_*^{U\mathfrak g}(R,M)</math>, where <math>\mathfrak g</math> is a [[Lie algebra]] over a commutative ring ''R'', ''M'' is a <math>\mathfrak g</math>-module, and <math>U\mathfrak g</math> is the [[universal enveloping algebra]].
*For a commutative ring ''R'' with a homomorphism onto a field ''k'', <math>\operatorname{Tor}_*^R(k,k)</math> is a graded-commutative [[Hopf algebra]] over ''k''.<ref>Avramov & Halperin (1986), section 4.7.</ref> (If ''R'' is a [[Noetherian local ring]] with residue field ''k'', then the dual Hopf algebra to <math>\operatorname{Tor}_*^R(k,k)</math> is [[Ext functor#Important special cases|Ext]]{{supsub|*|''R''}}(''k'',''k'').) As an algebra, <math>\operatorname{Tor}_*^R(k,k)</math> is the free graded-commutative divided power algebra on a graded vector space π<sub>*</sub>(''R'').<ref>Gulliksen & Levin (1969), Theorem 2.3.5; Sjödin (1980), Theorem 1.</ref> When ''k'' has [[characteristic of a field|characteristic]] zero, π<sub>*</sub>(''R'') can be identified with the [[André-Quillen homology]] ''D''<sub>*</sub>(''k''/''R'',''k'').<ref>Quillen (1970), section 7.</ref>
